summary: The cooking of the old capital Huế is bold and fiery, shaped by the style of the royal court — many small, refined dishes, each with its own dipping sauce.

bun-bo-hue.description: A deep, fiery noodle soup with a broth simmered from beef bones and pork trotter, scented with sả (lemongrass) and mắm ruốc (fermented shrimp/krill paste), served with thick round bún (rice noodles) — the culinary emblem of the old capital, far more forceful than northern phở.
keyIngredients: Beef bones, pork trotter, beef shank
Sả (lemongrass), mắm ruốc (fermented shrimp/krill paste), chilli-annatto oil
prepOutline: Simmer the beef bones and pork trotter with bruised sả (lemongrass)
Dissolve the mắm ruốc (fermented shrimp/krill paste), strain off the clear liquid and add it to the pot
Render annatto oil to give the broth its deep red colour
Blanch the bún (rice noodles) and lay the beef shank, trotter and blood on top
Ladle over the boiling broth and scatter with spring onion and coriander
bun-bo-hue.howToEat: Eaten hot, with a squeeze of lime and extra sa tế (chilli-oil paste) or mắm ruốc (fermented shrimp/krill paste) to your own tolerance for heat; crush the banana blossom and raw greens and drop them into the bowl for a cool, crisp bite against the fierce broth.

com-hen.description: Cold rice tossed with stir-fried hến (tiny freshwater clams), their cooking liquor, pork cracklings, peanuts and a great deal of raw greenery — the everyday dish of the Cồn Hến quarter of Huế, balanced between sour and hot.
keyIngredients: Hến (tiny freshwater clams — the meat and the cooking liquor)
Sa tế (chilli-oil paste), mắm ruốc (fermented shrimp/krill paste)
prepOutline: Boil the hến (tiny freshwater clams) and keep the clear cooking liquor
Stir-fry the clam meat with seasonings until fragrant
Toss the cold rice with the raw greens, pork cracklings and peanuts
Ladle over the hot clam liquor and add sa tế (chilli-oil paste) and mắm ruốc (fermented shrimp/krill paste)
com-hen.howToEat: Mix everything together thoroughly before eating and ladle on more hot clam liquor so the rice does not dry out; it is only complete if you eat it as hot as Huế taste demands.

banh-khoai.description: The Huế version of bánh xèo — smaller, thicker and crisper than the southern kind, filled with shrimp, pork and bean sprouts and eaten with a distinctive nước lèo of liver and peanut rather than the usual sweet-and-sour nước mắm (Vietnamese fish sauce).
keyIngredients: Huế nước lèo (a sauce of pork liver, peanut and sesame)
Raw greens, sour star fruit, green banana
prepOutline: Mix the rice batter with nghệ (turmeric) to bring up the yellow colour
Pour the batter into a hot pan and add the shrimp, pork and bean sprouts
Fold the cake in half once the edges are golden and crisp
Mix the liver-and-peanut nước lèo particular to Huế
banh-khoai.howToEat: Roll it up with raw greens, sour star fruit and green banana, then dip it deep into the Huế nước lèo — the rich, nutty sauce is the single biggest difference from southern bánh xèo.

banh-beo-nam-loc.description: The three Huế court cakes usually served together on one tray: bánh bèo steamed in little bowls and topped with tôm cháy (dried shrimp floss), bánh nậm wrapped flat in a leaf around a shrimp-and-pork filling, and bánh lọc, clear as glass around shrimp and pork, wrapped in lá chuối (banana leaf).
keyIngredients: Rice flour (for bánh bèo and bánh nậm), tapioca starch (for bánh lọc)
Tôm cháy (dried shrimp floss), minced pork belly
Lá chuối (banana leaf) or lá dong (dong leaf) for wrapping
Diluted nước mắm (Vietnamese fish sauce) with chilli
prepOutline: Steam the rice batter in little bowls (bánh bèo) or in leaf wrappers (bánh nậm)
Pound the tôm cháy (dried shrimp floss) fine and scatter it over the bánh bèo
Enclose shrimp and pork in clear tapioca dough and steam it (bánh lọc)
Arrange all three on a tray or plate and serve with nước mắm (Vietnamese fish sauce) and chilli
banh-beo-nam-loc.howToEat: Spoon the diluted nước mắm (Vietnamese fish sauce) with chilli straight over each kind of cake and eat them in small mouthfuls — the 'ăn chơi' style of Huế court food, meant for grazing rather than for filling you up.
